::: {#def-topological-space}
## Topology and Topological Space

A *topological space* is a pair $(S, \mathcal{T})$, where $S$ is a set and $\mathcal{T}$ is a collection of subsets of $S$ (called *open sets*) satisfying:

(a) $\varnothing, S \in \mathcal{T}$,
(b) any union of members of $\mathcal{T}$ is in $\mathcal{T}$,
(c) any finite intersection of members of $\mathcal{T}$ is in $\mathcal{T}$.

We call $\mathcal{T}$ a *topology* on $S$. A set $F \subset S$ is *closed* if $S \setminus F \in \mathcal{T}$.
:::

::: {#def-metric-space}
## Metric and Metric Spaces

A *metric* on a set $S$ is a function $d: S \times S \to [0, \infty)$ that satisfies

(a) $d(x_1, x_2) = 0$ if and only if $x_1 = x_2$,
(b) $d(x_1, x_2) = d(x_2, x_1)$, and
(c) $d(x_1, x_3) \leq d(x_1, x_2) + d(x_2, x_3)$,

for $x_1, x_2, x_3 \in S$. We call the pair $(S, d)$ a *metric space*.
:::

::: {#thm-metric-topology}
A metric space $(S,d)$ induces a topological space $(S, \mathcal{T}_d)$, where
$$
\mathcal{T}_d \coloneqq \{E \subset S : E \text{ is open with respect to } d\}.
$$
:::

::: {#def-open-closed}
## Openness and Closedness

Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space with $E \subset S$. Then $E$ is said to be *open* if for every $e \in E$, there exists an $\epsilon > 0$ such that $\{x \in S: d(x, e) < \epsilon\} \subset E$. The subset $E$ is *closed* if $S \setminus E$ is open.
:::

::: {.remark}
The definitions of openness or closedness in topological spaces are equivalent with ones in metric spaces.
:::

::: {#def-closure}
## Closure

Let $S$ be a topological space and $A \subset S$. The *closure* $\overline{A}$ of $A$ is the intersection of all closed subsets of $S$ containing $A$, i.e., the smallest closed set containing $A$.
:::

::: {#def-interior}
## Interior

Let $S$ be a topological space and $A \subset S$. The *interior* $A^\circ$ of $A$ is the union of all open subsets of $S$ contained in $A$, i.e., the largest open set contained in $A$.
:::

::: {#def-boundary}
## Boundary

Let $S$ be a topological space and $A \subset S$. The *boundary* $\partial A$ of $A$ is
$$
\partial A = \overline A \setminus A^\circ.
$$
:::

::: {#def-convergence}
## Convergence

Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A sequence $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset S$ *converges* to a limit $x \in S$ if for any $\epsilon > 0$ there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$
d(x_n, x) < \epsilon, \quad \forall n \geq N.
$$
It is denoted as $x_n \to x$ (as $n \to \infty$).
:::

::: {.remark}
In a metric space, a limit is unique.
:::

::: {#def-cauchy}
## Cauchy Sequence

Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A sequence $\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset S$ is called a *Cauchy sequence* if for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$
\sup_{m, n \geq N} d(x_m, x_n) < \epsilon.
$$
:::

::: {#thm-cauchy-convergence}
Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space, and let $\{x_n\} \subset S$ be a sequence.

(a) If $\{x_n\}$ converges, then $\{x_n\}$ is a Cauchy sequence.
(b) If $\{x_n\}$ is a Cauchy sequence and has a convergent subsequence, then $\{x_n\}$ converges.
:::

::: {#def-completeness}
## Completeness

A metric space $(S, d)$ is *complete* if every Cauchy sequence in $S$ converges to a point of $S$. A subset $E \subset S$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence in $E$ converges to a point of $E$.
:::

::: {#def-open-cover}
## Open Cover

Let $S$ be a topological space and $E \subset S$. An *open cover* of $E$ is a collection $\{G_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}$ of open subsets of $S$ such that $E \subset \bigcup_{\alpha \in I} G_\alpha$. A *subcover* is a subcollection $\{G_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in J}$, $J \subset I$, which is still an open cover of $E$.
:::

::: {#def-compactness}
## Compactness

A topological space $S$ is *compact* if every open cover has a finite subcover. A subset $E \subset S$ is compact if every open cover of $E$ has a finite subcover.
:::

::: {#def-lindelof}
## Lindelöf Space

A topological space $S$ is called a *Lindelöf space* if every open cover has a countable subcover. A subset $E \subset S$ is Lindelöf if every open cover of $E$ has a countable subcover.
:::

::: {#def-countable}
## Countable Set

A set $A$ is *countable* if there exists an injective map $f: A \to \mathbb{N}$. A set that is not countable is *uncountable*.
:::

::: {#def-dense}
## Dense Set

Let $S$ be a topological space. A subset $A \subset S$ is *dense* in $S$ if, for the closure $\overline A$,
$$
\overline A = S.
$$
:::

::: {#def-separability}
## Separability

A topological space $S$ is *separable* if it contains a countable dense subset. A subset $E \subset S$ is separable if it contains a countable dense subset $D \subset E$.
:::

::: {#thm-closed-subset}
Let $S$ be a topological space. Then, the following hold.

(a) If $S$ is a compact space, then a closed subset $E \subset S$ is compact.
(b) If $S$ is a Lindelöf space, then a closed subset $E \subset S$ is Lindelöf.
:::

::: {#thm-separable-lindelof}
Let $S$ be a metric space. Then, $S$ is separable if and only if $S$ is Lindelöf.
:::

::: {#def-boundedness}
## Boundedness

Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A subset $E \subset S$ is *bounded* if there exists $r > 0$ such that
$$
d(x, y) < r, \quad \forall x, y \in E.
$$
:::

::: {#def-total-boundedness}
## Total Boundedness

Let $(S, d)$ be a metric space. A subset $E \subset S$ is *totally bounded* if, for any $\epsilon > 0$, there exist finitely many points $x_1, \dots, x_n \in E$ such that
$$
E \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^n B_\epsilon(x_i),
$$
where $B_\epsilon(x_i) = \{x \in S: d(x_i, x) < \epsilon\}$.
:::

::: {#thm-totally-bounded}
Every totally bounded set is bounded. The converse is not necessarily true.
:::

::: {#def-sequential-compactness}
## Sequential Compactness

Let $S$ be a topological space. A subset $E \subset S$ is *sequentially compact* if every sequence in $E$ has a convergent subsequence in $E$.
:::

::: {#thm-heine-borel}
## Heine-Borel Theorem

For a set $E$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^k$, the following are equivalent.

(a) $E$ is compact.
(b) $E$ is closed and bounded.
:::

::: {#thm-generalized-heine-borel}
## Generalized Heine-Borel Theorem

For a set $E$ in a metric space $S$, the following are equivalent.

(a) $E$ is compact.
(b) $E$ is sequentially compact.
(c) $E$ is complete and totally bounded.
:::

::: {#def-polish}
## Polish Space

A *Polish space* is a topological space that is separable and metrizable in such a way that it becomes complete.
:::

::: {.remark}
More explicitly, a topological space $(S, \mathcal{T})$ is called *Polish* if $(S,\mathcal{T})$ is separable and there exists a metric $d$ on $S$ such that $\mathcal{T}$ is the topology induced by $d$ and $(S, d)$ is complete.
:::
